prize_parts.citation: For showing how differences in productivity across firms shape who exports and invests abroad, and for reworking the theory of gains from trade around firm-level selection and reallocation.

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed the unit of analysis in international economics from countries and industries to firms. Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) on exports versus FDI, together with Helpman's broader work on trade under imperfect competition and firm organisation, completes the intellectual line. The framework explains exporter premia, selection and within-industry reallocation. It adds a gains-from-trade channel that did not exist in the earlier theory. It has also given rise to a very large body of firm-level empirical work and is now standard in teaching, policy analysis, and in macro and IO applications. It is over twenty years old and has been tested repeatedly against transaction-level and firm-level data, so maturity is not a concern. The credit is also reasonably concentrated: two names capture the core model and its first major extension. My opening ranking holds after reading my colleagues' statements, and I do not think the discussion has weakened this case.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. Bernard and Jensen on exporter premia, Eaton and Kortum, and Hopenhayn on firm dynamics all have strong claims to adjacent work, and none of them is credited on this ballot line. Redding is credited on the list but left out here because his main contributions are quantitative and spatial extensions, which leaves the three-name list incomplete. Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the earlier new trade theory. Helpman's candidacy is also split with B049. Finally, the Arkolakis-Costinot-Rodriguez-Clare results show that the welfare gains from selection depend heavily on functional-form assumptions and may be smaller than the original theory suggested.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B014 sixth. He regards Melitz (2003) as the central paper but sees overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize and notes that Helpman's credit is split with B049. He also asks whether the work is a theoretical refinement or a discovery.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, but I think the two achievements are distinct. Krugman's prize recognised scale economies, product differentiation and trade patterns, all with representative firms. Melitz moved the object of analysis to productivity-sorted firms and put selection and reallocation at the centre of the gains from trade. This also produced testable predictions that were then confirmed in micro data, which is why I see it as a discovery and not just a refinement. On the split with B049, I would cite Helpman here for the heterogeneous-firm and exports-versus-FDI work. That is a coherent and separate rationale from his political economy of trade policy, so I do not think the two candidacies weaken each other much.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 second. He values the end of the long gap since Krugman, but flags the claims of Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum and the Arkolakis et al. critique of the size of welfare gains.
responses.response: I agree with both qualifications and treat them differently. The Arkolakis et al. result qualifies how large the selection channel is under particular structural assumptions. It does not undo the discovery, and it only became a sharp question because the heterogeneous-firm framework made the welfare calculation tractable. The attribution point is harder and I do not dismiss it. I would keep the citation narrow, on firm selection and the gains from trade, so that the empirical exporter-premia and quantitative-trade lines are not claimed by implication. Whether that is enough to answer the Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum claims is something I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B045 first and B014 second. He regards B014 as mature and influential, with Melitz central and Helpman strong, but sees Redding's contribution to welfare gains as potentially blurring the credit.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz and Helpman is the cleanest pair and that adding Redding would weaken the core-discovery rationale. On B045, I also rank the BLP framework highly, and I place it third. My reservation is that a prize there raises the framing and attribution questions he himself lists: BLP versus the broader structural IO agenda, and Bresnahan's claim. B014 faces a smaller version of that problem. I do not think the BLP case is weaker on scientific merit. I prefer B014 because its credited core is more cleanly defined under the two-to-three-name constraint.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He argues that the China-shock work has credible designs, replicated effects, and influence well beyond economics, and he leaves out Katz.
responses.response: I agree that B009 is the strongest rival, and I ranked it second on scientific grounds. The research designs are credible and the policy reach is real. My reservations are about the shape of the prize. The achievement bundles at least three strands: skill-biased change, tasks, and trade shocks. It overlaps in subject with Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024), and the shift-share inference and persistence questions are still debated. Swapping Dorn for Katz makes the citation cleaner on the trade-shock side, but it drops the technology and wage-structure strand and makes the prize mainly about the China shock. A prize for B009 as a whole needs Autor, Hanson and Katz, and then Dorn's omission is a real cost. I regard B014 as having a more compact and better-bounded core.

uncertainties: Whether Bernard-Jensen, Eaton-Kortum or Hopenhayn have priority claims strong enough that a Melitz-Helpman citation overstates the novelty of the heterogeneous-firm framework.
Whether the quantitative-trade line (B043, which is not on this shortlist) is the better-recognised frame for firm-level trade research.
How much of the headline welfare gain from selection survives the Arkolakis et al. critique, and whether that should affect the citation wording.
Whether B009 or B014 is the better-bounded achievement when the three-name cap is applied, given the overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes for B009 and with Krugman's 2008 prize for B014.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted candidate is apparent from the supplied profile. For transparency: I work on exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and pricing under imperfect competition, which is adjacent to B014 and B011, and I co-authored an IJIO 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. None of these is a link to a credited name. My spouse is a Swedish politician. This is a public fact only, and no bearing on any shortlisted achievement is apparent from the profile.
